questions.text: When a person advances to the next mode, what do they actually do, and who checks that the gate is met: the rollout controller, or the person?
questions.about: person advances, gate A met / gate B met

questions.text: Where do the usage events come from, and how does the new engine read them in shadow without affecting the old engine?
questions.about: shadow: Reads the same usage events and writes to the shadow store

questions.text: Who or what runs the nightly comparison, and where do its results go? How does a mismatch become 'resolved'?
questions.about: Nightly comparison / Unresolved mismatch in both

questions.text: When a rollback starts, what exactly sets the rollback marker and when? Does the controller set it at RB_Halt, and how do workers see it?
How does the on-call person trigger a manual rollback, and how does the system detect the 2 percent failure rate and start the automatic one?
questions.about: RB_Halt: on-call manual, or auto when charge failure rate over 2 pct in 10 min

questions.text: During RB_Halt to RB_Handover nobody is charging. How long can that take, and what happens to customers whose charges are due in that time?
questions.about: One charger at a time / Nothing dropped

questions.text: In RB_Reconcile, what happens when the ledger and the payment provider disagree, for example the provider shows a charge that the ledger lacks?
questions.about: RB_Reconcile: every charge matched to ledger and provider

questions.text: What is day 35 counted from, and why is it 35 days?

answers.text: The person asks the controller to advance; the controller checks the gate from the rollout record and refuses if unmet, then sets the flag. Reason: the gate counters already live in the controller's record, and a machine check avoids human error. Added to the Forward moves note.

Both engines read the same usage event log, read-only, each with its own read position, so the new engine cannot affect the old. This follows the brief's rule that shadow reads the same events. Added to the mode notes.

The rollout controller runs the nightly comparison and stores daily results in the rollout record; that part is my design. How a mismatch becomes resolved is not defined in the brief and I have no defended rule (fix, or Finance acceptance). Added as open point 5.

The controller sets the marker at the very start of RB_Halt, before stopping charging. Workers read it from the rollout record before every new-engine charge. Reason: the flag alone cannot signal a halt and must stay unchanged until handover. Added.

On-call runs a rollback command on the controller. The controller watches charge outcomes and starts the automatic rollback when the failure rate exceeds 2% in a 10-minute window. Having one component own both triggers keeps the single-rollback rule enforceable. Added under Rollback steps.

The duration is not known and depends on reconcile and reprocess size. Due charges are queued under idempotency keys and charged late by the old engine at handover, never skipped. Added to Nothing dropped and as open point 6 (possible maximum delay).

The provider is the truth about money moved. A provider charge missing from the ledger gets a ledger entry added. A ledger charge the provider has no record of, once confirmed by lookup, is treated as due and stays queued. Reason: this avoids double charging and avoids dropping a due charge. Added to the RB_Reconcile row.

Day 35 is counted from entering new_only. It equals the usage event log retention in the brief: after 35 days the skipped events are gone, so reprocessing and rollback are impossible. Added a note under the gates.

questions.text: When the flag moves from shadow to both, the old engine stops charging and the new one starts. How is that switch made so that no customer is charged by both or by neither at that moment?
questions.about: shadow --> both : person advances, gate A met

questions.text: What does it mean for the old engine to be 'Stopped' in new_only? Who stops it, and what happens to its read position in the usage event log?
What are the 'workers' that read the flag and the rollback marker? Do they run the engines, and how quickly do they notice a flag or marker change?
questions.about: Mode: the billing_mode flag in the config service

questions.text: At RB_Handover, how does the old engine find out which queued charges are due? Where is the queue kept and who reads it?
In both mode, what is compared against what, given the old engine writes only to the shadow store and the new engine writes the ledger? What is a 'mismatch' there?
What counts as 'in-flight charges drained' for moving from RB_Halt to RB_Reconcile? Is there a time limit for waiting on in-flight charge calls?

answers.text: The switch is a handover too, so I reuse the charge hold: the controller sets it, in-flight charge calls finish or time out, it sets the flag, then clears the hold. Nobody charges during the gap, so nobody is charged twice. Charges due in the gap are charged late by the new engine, which skips anything already in the ledger, so nobody is missed. Added to Forward moves and to the hold description. The other two forward moves do not change the charger.

Stopped means workers no longer run the old engine when the flag says new_only. The flag stops it, so no one has to stop it by hand. Its read position stays where it was, and RB_Reprocess resumes from there to replay the skipped events. Added to the new_only row.

Workers are the billing workers from the brief, which run the engines. Each follows the flag, and the hold is read from the rollout record before every charge. How fast they notice a flag change is not known. Correctness does not depend on it, because the hold is read at charge time, but the length of the pause does. Added a line under modes, the hold description and open point 7.

The charge queue lives in the rollout record next to the ledger. After the hold is cleared, the old engine's workers read it and charge each entry that is due and not already in the ledger. Reason: it must survive restarts and sit beside the ledger so the ledger check is cheap. Added to the record list.

Checked against the brief. In both, the new engine's ledger invoices are compared with the old engine's shadow-store invoices, and a mismatch is the same per-customer total differing by more than one cent. In shadow it is the old engine's ledger against the new engine's shadow store. Added to the Nightly comparison note.

Drained means every charge call has returned or timed out. A timed-out call has an unknown outcome and goes to RB_Reconcile for a provider lookup. The timeout value is not set and I have no defended number. Added the definition to RB_Halt and open point 7.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one concrete case: a rollout that runs forward from old_only to new_only, with an automatic rollback from `both`. That is the main flow in the document.

1. **Start state.** The `billing_mode` flag in the config service is `old_only`. Billing workers read the flag to pick an engine. The old engine computes invoices, writes the ledger and charges. The new engine is off. The flag is the only thing workers read to choose an engine.

2. **old_only to shadow.** A person asks the rollout controller to advance, and the controller sets the flag to `shadow`. The document names no gate for this move. It does not change who charges, so no charge hold is needed. Workers now run both engines. The old engine still computes, writes the ledger and charges. The new engine reads the same usage event log, keeps its own read position, and writes invoices to the shadow store. It never charges and never writes the ledger.

3. **Nightly comparison in shadow.** The controller runs a nightly job. It compares per-customer invoice totals from the old engine's ledger against the new engine's shadow-store invoices. A mismatch is a difference of more than one cent. Each day's result is stored in the rollout record. That record is a durable record kept next to the ledger and written by the controller. If the job fails or has no data, that day does not count and the consecutive-day count resets. New-engine errors in shadow are recorded but never trigger a rollback.

4. **Shadow to both (gate A).** After 7 consecutive days under 0.1% mismatch and at least 5,000 invoices compared, a person asks the controller to advance. The controller checks gate A against the rollout record and refuses if it is not met. This move changes the charger from old to new, so the controller does the following in order:
   - It sets the charge hold, so no worker charges.
   - It waits for in-flight charge calls to finish or time out.
   - It sets the flag to `both`.
   - It clears the hold.

   Workers read the hold from the rollout record before every charge. This also protects against a worker that has not yet seen the new flag. Charges that fall due during the hold are charged late by the new engine. It skips any (customer, billing period) already in the ledger.

5. **Running in both.** The new engine computes, writes the ledger and charges. The old engine keeps computing, but only into the shadow store, so it stays current. The nightly comparison now checks the new engine's ledger against the old engine's shadow store. Every charge uses the key (customer, billing period). The ledger is checked before charging, and the provider rejects repeats.

6. **Failure: automatic rollback from both.** The controller watches charge outcomes. If the failure rate is over 2% in any 10-minute window, it starts a rollback itself and on-call is notified. On-call can also start one manually with a rollback command. Only one rollback runs at a time, and a second trigger is ignored. A forward move cannot interrupt a rollback.

7. **RB_Halt.** The controller sets the charge hold. It waits until every in-flight charge call has returned or timed out. Charges that come due meanwhile go into the charge queue under their idempotency keys. They are held, not dropped. The current rollback step and its trigger are recorded in the rollout record, so a controller restart resumes from the recorded step. Each step is safe to repeat.

8. **RB_Reconcile.** Every (customer, billing period) charge is matched between the ledger and the payment provider. An unknown outcome, including a timeout, is looked up at the provider first and never retried blind. The rules are:
   - If the provider shows a charge the ledger lacks, add the ledger entry.
   - If the ledger shows a charge the provider has no record of, once the lookup confirms that, treat it as due and leave it in the queue.
   - If an outcome is still unknown, stay in the step, retry and page on-call. The hold stays set.

9. **Source check.** Once everything matches, the flow branches on where the rollback started. From `both`, it goes straight to handover, because the old engine never stopped. From `new_only`, it goes to RB_Reprocess first.

10. **RB_Handover.** The controller sets `billing_mode` to `old_only` as the last action, then clears the hold. The old engine then charges the queued charges that are due and not yet in the ledger, each exactly once. Gates reset, so the 7-day and 14-day counts go back to zero. The rollout must go through `shadow` again.

11. **The other forward path, if no rollback happens.** After 14 days in `both` with no unresolved mismatches, and with Finance sign-off, a person advances to `new_only` through the controller, which checks gate B. No hold is needed. The old engine stops, and its read position in the usage event log stays where it was. Day 35 is counted from entering `new_only`. Before day 35, the same failure triggers apply and a rollback goes via RB_Halt, then RB_Reconcile, then RB_Reprocess. In RB_Reprocess the old engine replays the usage events it skipped, in non-charging mode, into the shadow store. A failed step is retried and on-call is paged. After that comes handover. At day 35 or later, a person can decommission the old engine. That is terminal and rollback is impossible. If the failure rate is exceeded then, on-call is paged to fix forward.

12. **Rollback from shadow.** This is the simple case. On-call triggers it manually. RB_StopNew turns the new engine off and sets the flag to `old_only`. Gates reset. There is no reconcile, because the new engine never charged.
gaps: What counts as the gate for old_only to shadow: the document names no gate or precondition for that first move.

How workers actually detect the flag and read the hold. The document only says the hold is read from the rollout record before every charge. How the charge queue is stored and drained, and how the old engine gets the queued charges, is not described.
What 'resolved' means for a mismatch, and who records it. This blocks gate B and so blocks the both to new_only step (the document lists this as an open point).
How the controller learns that in-flight charge calls have finished or timed out, and what the timeout value is. This sets how long RB_Halt and the shadow to both switch wait.
How long RB_Reprocess takes, and the safety margin before day 35 for starting a rollback from new_only. The document says it needs a number.
The minimum sample size for the 2% failure rate trigger. As written, a burst of failures on very few charges could trigger a rollback.
How a person's 'advance' or Finance sign-off is recorded and authorised, meaning who is allowed to do it and through what interface.
How the 7-day and 14-day counters are computed from the daily results when a day is skipped or fails, beyond saying the consecutive count resets.
What happens to the shadow store contents and the old engine's read position after handover from both, and whether the shadow store is cleared when the rollout re-enters shadow.
